description: Power, authority and Weber’s three types: traditional, charismatic and rational-legal.
content_html:
Power and Authority: Key Concepts

In sociology, power and authority are closely related but distinct concepts. Power refers to the capacity to get others to do what you want, regardless of whether they consent — this can include coercion, force or threat. Authority refers to power that is considered legitimate: people comply because they believe the person or institution exercising power has the right to do so. A police officer who physically restrains someone exercises power; a judge who imposes a sentence exercises authority because the sentence is backed by a legal framework that most people accept as legitimate.

Max Weber (1947) distinguished three distinct types of authority based on the different grounds on which people accept another’s right to exercise power over them. These three types — traditional, charismatic and rational-legal — are among the most important concepts in the sociology of power and are directly assessed in your exam.

Key Fact

Weber’s three types of legitimate authority are: traditional (based on custom and inherited status), charismatic (based on exceptional personal qualities) and rational-legal (based on formal rules and offices). Each has a different source of legitimacy and different implications for how power operates in society.

Weber’s Three Types of Authority

Traditional authority is the oldest form of legitimate power. It rests on the belief that certain customs, institutions and rulers have always existed and therefore have an established right to exercise authority. Obedience is owed to the person who holds a traditional office, not to any particular set of rules. The clearest UK example is the monarchy: the legitimacy of the Crown rests on hereditary succession and centuries of custom, not on any written mandate from the people or formal qualifications. The power of landlords over tenants in feudal society was similarly traditional.

Charismatic authority derives not from rules or tradition but from the personal qualities of the individual — their vision, magnetism, communication skills or perceived special destiny. Followers obey because they believe in the leader as a person, not because of the office they hold. Charismatic authority is inherently unstable because it depends on the continued belief of followers and cannot easily be passed on. When a charismatic leader dies or loses followers’ trust, their authority typically either disappears or is “routinised” into traditional or rational-legal form. A religious leader or a political leader who builds a movement through personal appeal provides a sociological illustration.

Rational-legal authority is the form Weber saw as characteristic of modern bureaucratic societies. Its legitimacy rests on the acceptance of formal rules, laws and procedures. People obey not because of custom or personal charisma but because they accept the legitimacy of the legal framework. Authority is attached to offices rather than individuals — an elected Member of Parliament or a judge exercises authority because of the office they hold under the constitutional framework, not because of who they personally are. Weber saw the growth of rational-legal authority as fundamental to modern capitalist societies.

Students frequently apply the wrong type to examples. Key tests: Is the authority based on rules and formal offices? → rational-legal. Is it based on custom and who you were born as? → traditional. Is it based purely on personality and personal devotion to the leader? → charismatic. Common errors: labelling a popularly elected Prime Minister as “charismatic” because they are popular — they hold rational-legal authority because their power rests on formal electoral rules, not personal devotion. Calling a hereditary peer “rational-legal” — they hold traditional authority because their position is inherited, not based on a formal qualification or election.

Formal and Informal Sources of Power

Weber’s three types of authority are all forms of formal power — power that operates through official channels. But power is also exercised informally. Informal power operates outside official structures. Economic power — an employer’s ability to dismiss or reward workers — is a form of informal power not necessarily embedded in law. Cultural prestige can shape behaviour without any formal authority. Within family relationships, patriarchal power can operate informally through gendered expectations and the division of domestic labour. Weber also identified social closure as a mechanism of informal power: professional bodies that control entry to high-status occupations restrict access to valued resources.

Agencies of Social Control

Power in society is exercised not just by individuals but through agencies of social control — institutions that monitor and regulate behaviour to maintain social order. Agencies of social control can be formal or informal. Formal agencies have official, legally defined powers: the police enforce criminal law; the courts administer justice; the prison system punishes offenders. Schools exercise formal authority over young people through attendance laws and disciplinary powers. Informal agencies exercise social control through norms, peer pressure and socialisation rather than legal compulsion: the family, peer groups and the media all shape behaviour by rewarding conformity and stigmatising deviance. The distinction between formal and informal agencies is important because much social control is achieved informally, without the direct exercise of legal power.

Functionalists tend to view legitimate authority — especially rational-legal authority — as a functional necessity for social order. The 2024 examiner report noted that stronger candidates understood that functionalists accept power differences exist but see them as “inevitable and necessary” for the smooth running of society. Authority structures serve the common good rather than any one group’s interests.

Marxists argue that in capitalist societies, authority structures ultimately serve the interests of the bourgeoisie. Ruling class ideology makes the state’s authority appear neutral and legitimate when in practice it protects the property rights and economic position of those who own the means of production. Weber’s rational-legal framework, from a Marxist perspective, obscures the class basis of state power.

Feminist sociologists argue that authority structures are patriarchal: historically, both traditional authority (inherited male power in monarchies and patriarchal families) and rational-legal authority (legal systems that long denied women voting rights and professional access) have operated to maintain male dominance. Walby’s identification of the state as one of the six structures of patriarchy is directly relevant here.

Key Fact

Weber’s three types of authority are frequently tested in 3-mark Identify and Describe and 4-mark Describe questions. Know the name, the source of legitimacy and at least one example of each. Do not call elected officials ‘charismatic’ — their authority is rational-legal because it derives from constitutional rules, not personal devotion.
exam_tip_html: On a 3-mark Identify and Describe question asking you to identify and describe a type of authority, students often name the correct type but give an inaccurate example or fail to describe what makes that form of authority legitimate. The mark scheme expects: the correct name (1 mark), the source of legitimacy explained (1 mark), and a developed example (1 mark). For rational-legal authority: name it, explain it rests on formal rules and offices rather than personality or custom, and give an example such as a judge or an elected MP. For a 12-mark Evaluate on whether power in modern society is exercised legitimately, structure your answer around the three Weberian types plus competing perspectives: functionalist (authority as socially necessary); Marxist (authority serving class interests); feminist (authority as patriarchal). Close with a supported judgement that weighs these perspectives against each other.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Weber distinguished power (the ability to make others comply regardless of consent) from authority (legitimate power that people accept as rightful). He identified three types: traditional (custom and inheritance), charismatic (exceptional personal qualities) and rational-legal (formal rules and offices).
  • Formal power operates through official institutions and legal frameworks; informal power operates through social relationships, economic position, cultural influence and norms. Social control is exercised by both formal agencies (police, courts, schools) and informal agencies (family, peer groups, media).
  • Functionalists see authority structures as necessary for social order; Marxists argue they serve ruling-class interests; feminists argue they have historically maintained male dominance and continue to reflect patriarchal values.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of authority is based on formal rules and offices, where people obey the rules rather than the individual?
A) Traditional authority
B) Charismatic authority
C) Informal authority
D) Rational-legal authority
Define the term 'authority' as used by sociologists.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that authority involves the exercise of power; 1 mark for specifying that it is considered legitimate — people accept or recognise the right of the person or institution to exercise power over them. Example: 'Authority is the exercise of power that is accepted as legitimate by those over whom it is exercised, meaning people comply because they recognise the right of the authority figure or institution to issue commands rather than simply because they are forced to obey.'

practice_questions.text: Identify and describe one of Weber's three types of authority.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly naming one of the three types (traditional, charismatic or rational-legal). 2 marks for a developed description of its source of legitimacy and a relevant example: e.g. 'Traditional authority is based on long-established custom and the inherited status of rulers — people obey because this is how authority has always operated, not because of any formal rule or personal quality. A UK example is the monarchy, where the Crown's legitimacy rests on hereditary succession over centuries rather than electoral mandate or personal charisma.'

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between formal and informal agencies of social control, using sociological examples.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks. Formal agencies of social control have official, legally defined powers — the police enforce criminal law, courts administer justice, schools exercise legal authority over attendance and discipline (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Informal agencies exercise control through norms, peer pressure and socialisation rather than legal compulsion — the family, peer groups and the media shape behaviour by rewarding conformity and stigmatising deviance (1 mark, developed 2 marks). Any two well-developed examples from different categories earn 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the view that power in modern British society is always exercised legitimately.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: at least two named perspectives developed in detail, both sides of the debate, sustained sociological vocabulary, supported judgement. Supporting the view: Weber's analysis of rational-legal authority as resting on accepted formal rules and offices — in modern bureaucratic societies people broadly accept the authority of elected governments and legal systems. Functionalist view that authority structures serve the common good. Contrasting: Marxist view that authority ultimately serves bourgeois class interests, making it appear neutral via ideology; feminist view that patriarchal structures mean authority has historically excluded women and continues to reflect male-dominated norms. Named sociologists and concepts (rational-legal, traditional, charismatic, patriarchy, ruling class ideology) used throughout. Supported judgement.

Secure: Both sides covered, named sociologists referenced, judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant points but mostly one-sided or undeveloped; some vocabulary; conclusion assertive.

Emerging: Basic points, mostly description, few named sociologists, little judgement.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate Weber's theory of authority as an explanation of how power operates in modern society.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: full range of relevant arguments. Weber's three types explained and evaluated in depth — traditional (custom, monarchy), charismatic (personal qualities, instability), rational-legal (modern bureaucratic societies, offices not persons). Strengths of the Weberian framework: recognises diversity of authority types, explains how power is accepted beyond mere force. At least two contrasting critiques developed: Marxist critique (rational-legal authority obscures class basis of state power, ruling class ideology); feminist critique (all three types have historically maintained patriarchal power; Walby's state structure of patriarchy). Functionalist view also considered (authority as socially necessary). Named sociologists and precise vocabulary throughout. Supported judgement weighing Weber's framework against alternatives.

Secure: Most arguments present; both strengths and critiques of Weber; named sociologists; judgement offered.

Developing: Relevant but mostly descriptive of Weber without evaluation; some vocabulary; weak conclusion.

Emerging: Basic description of one type of authority; few named theorists; little evaluation.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of authority is based on long-established custom and the inherited status of rulers?
Charismatic authority is described as inherently unstable because it depends on the continued _____ of followers.
Power exercised through official institutions, laws or constitutional offices is called _____ power.
Weber's type of authority based on formal rules, laws and impersonal procedures is called _____ authority.
Match each type of authority to its source of legitimacy:
right: Long-established custom and inherited status — it has always been this way
Exceptional personal qualities and followers' personal devotion to the individual leader
Formal rules, laws and impersonal procedures — authority attached to offices, not persons

flashcard_questions.a: The ability to make others comply, even against their wishes, whether or not this is considered legitimate.
Power that is accepted as legitimate — people obey because they recognise the right of the person or institution to exercise it.
Authority based on long-established custom and inherited status, accepted because it has always been this way.

flashcard_questions.q: Give a UK example of traditional authority.
flashcard_questions.a: The monarchy — the Crown's legitimacy rests on hereditary succession and centuries of custom.
Authority based on exceptional personal qualities of an individual leader who inspires devotion in followers.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is charismatic authority described as unstable?
flashcard_questions.a: It depends on continued personal devotion to the leader and cannot easily be passed on after their death or loss of credibility.
Authority based on formal rules and offices — people obey the rules, not the individual; authority is attached to positions, not persons.

flashcard_questions.q: Give a UK example of rational-legal authority.
flashcard_questions.a: A judge or elected MP — their authority derives from the constitutional and legal framework, not personal qualities.
Power exercised through official institutions, laws or constitutional offices, backed by formal rules and the state.
Power exercised through social relationships, economic position, cultural influence or norms rather than official institutions.
The process by which groups restrict access to their privileges to their own members, excluding outsiders.

flashcard_questions.q: How do Marxists critique Weber's rational-legal authority?
flashcard_questions.a: They argue it obscures the class basis of state power — legal authority appears neutral but protects ruling-class economic interests.

glossary_terms.definition: The ability to make others do what you want, even against their wishes, whether or not this is considered legitimate.
Power that is accepted as legitimate — people obey because they recognise the right of the person or institution to exercise power over them.
Authority based on long-established custom and the inherited status of rulers, accepted because it has always been this way.
Authority based on the exceptional personal qualities of an individual leader who inspires devotion and loyalty in followers.
Authority based on formal rules, laws and impersonal procedures; authority is attached to offices rather than to the persons who hold them.
Power exercised through official institutions, laws or constitutional offices, backed by formal rules and often sanctioned by the state.
Power exercised through social relationships, norms, economic position or cultural influence rather than through official institutions.
The process by which certain groups restrict access to privileges or resources to their own members, excluding outsiders.
